- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

cat > /root/spectral_collapse_ews/paper/introduction.tex << 'INTROEOF'
\section{Introduction}

Training language models on their own synthetic outputs across multiple generations leads to \emph{model collapse}, a progressive narrowing of the learned distribution that degrades generation quality~\cite{shumailov2024}.
Recent empirical and theoretical work reveals that this degradation is not linear: spectral contraction in representation spaces accelerates around generation 20~\cite{sigma2026}, tail distributions compound with each generation~\cite{shumailov2024}, and degradation rates double past inflection points in the synthetic proportion~\cite{calibration2025}.
This non-linear acceleration makes the \emph{timing} of corrective intervention as important as its magnitude.

The dominant mitigation strategy is mixing real data into the synthetic training pipeline.
Theoretical analyses identify optimal static mixing ratios, notably the golden ratio $\phi^{-1} \approx 0.618$~\cite{he2025golden}, and data accumulation strategies that prevent collapse in principle~\cite{gerstgrasser2024, garg2025}.
However, static ratios assume constant collapse pressure across generations, an assumption contradicted by the empirical evidence of non-linear acceleration.
Meanwhile, spectral monitoring tools like SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} diagnose collapse in rich detail but prescribe no intervention.
Adaptive sampling methods such as DCES~\cite{dces2026} redistribute \emph{within} the synthetic pool but do not control the global real-to-synthetic ratio.
No existing system closes the feedback loop from spectral diagnosis to adaptive real-data allocation.

We present, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop system connecting spectral collapse monitoring to budget-constrained adaptive mixing.
Our key insight is that a fixed real-data budget achieves improved collapse prevention when allocated \emph{temporally}, with real data concentrated at generations of peak collapse pressure rather than spread uniformly.
We monitor representational health via effective rank~\cite{rankme2023} and spectral log-volume of output embeddings, and feed the spectral log-volume signal into a proportional controller that adjusts the real-data fraction generation-by-generation while guaranteeing total budget adherence.
The design is budget-fixed by construction: our method and the uniform baseline consume identical amounts of real data, isolating the effect of temporal allocation.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item We provide the first spectral-level characterization of recursive synthetic training collapse and identify three distinct phases through joint tracking of effective rank, spectral log-volume, perplexity, and HellaSwag accuracy (Section~\ref{sec:spectral_trajectory}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0_metrics}).
\item We show that spectral log-volume serves as an early warning signal (EWS) for collapse: it declines before effective rank and exhibits greater temporal lead in larger models (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation}).
\item We introduce a budget-constrained proportional controller driven by spectral log-volume decline rate that reallocates a fixed real-data budget temporally, and validate improved perplexity and downstream accuracy over uniform and scheduled baselines (Section~\ref{sec:controller}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0_metrics}).
\end{itemize}

Our experiments on Pythia-410M across 10 recursive generations show that spectral-guided adaptive allocation achieves [X] lower perplexity and [Y\%] higher HellaSwag accuracy compared to uniform allocation with identical total real-data consumption.
In addition to fixed uniform and spectral-guided adaptive conditions, we include open-loop heuristic schedules (e.g., linear-increasing allocation) to isolate the incremental value of closed-loop feedback.
These results establish that \emph{when} real data is introduced matters, not just \emph{how much}. This finding supports the case for closed-loop intervention in synthetic training pipelines.
INTROEOF
